Introduction
This handbook is designed as a resource for guiding Physics De-
partment PhD students through their graduate careers. It is not in-
tended as a substitute for frequent meetings between the student
and the Physics Department’s faculty and staff, especially with the
Graduate Program Coordinator (GPC), Graduate Student Tracking
Committee (GSTC) and the student’s Supervisory Committee (SC)
(which includes the student’s major professor).
Note well, it is the responsibility of each graduate student to un-
derstand the policies, regulations, and procedures of the School of
Graduate Studies (SGS) and the Physics Department. Furthermore,
it is the responsibility of each graduate student to make sure that the
milestones of the program are achieved in a timely fashion.

USU PhD Program – General Requirements
The USU requirements for any PhD Degree program are
summarized below. Most of this information has been gleaned from
the USU Catalog; relevant sections include the
School of Graduate Studies Catalog and the
USU Catalog: Physics PhD.
Keep in mind that if a conflict exists between the information found
here and that provided by the Catalog or School of Graduate Studies
(SGS), then the Catalog and SGS are the authoritative sources.
1.1 Full Time Status
The following summarize the requirements for maintain-
ing status as a full-time PhD student.
• Acceptance by the Department with the concurrence of the Vice
Provost of Graduate Studies.
• Registered for 9 or more semester credits; or
• Registered for 6 or more credits if employed as a graduate assis-
tant for 15 or more hours a week; or
• Registered for 3 graduate credits with all required coursework
completed and only the research component of the degree re-
maining (Students registered for 3 credits must have an approved
Program of Study and approved Full-Time at 3 Credit form); or
• Registered for at least 3 graduate credits during the semester of
the Dissertation Defense Examination.

• Domestic doctoral students will be given until the last day of the
next semester (known as a “grace” semester) following the defense
to finish degree requirements. If a student has not completed all
degree requirements by the end of the grace semester, the student
must pay a $100 Late Completion Fee for each semester following
the grace semester. If working with faculty involves more than
routine submission of the dissertation, registration for 3 or more
credits is required.
Furthermore, if all degree requirements are not completed
within the grace semester following a successful defense, then
the major professor, with support of all members of the super-
visory committee, must submit an appeal to the Vice Provost
of Graduate Studies, justifying why the student should not be
required to defend the dissertation a second time.
• An equivalent of the grace period is available to international
doctoral students. Please see the link above for details.
1.2 Credit / Grade Requirements
The following summarizes the semester credit require-
ments associated with the Physics PhD program.
• 60 credit hour minimum [including minimum 18 hours disserta-
tion research (PHYS 7970)] beyond a bachelors degree; or
• 30 credit hour minimum [including minimum 12 hours disserta-
tion research (PHYS 7970)] beyond a master’s degree;
• Graduate students are required to maintain at least a 3.0 GPA
for degree-program courses. Grades of C− or lower will not be
accepted for a graduate degree.
• Class credits must be revalidated if more than 8 years have
elapsed before completion of degree. The student’s supervi-
sory committee (SC)1 is responsible for developing and submitting 1

and include the Vice Provost of Graduate Studies and the student’s

• Up to 12 semester credit hours (post bachelor’s degree) obtained
prior to USU matriculation may be transferred from another ac-
credited institution. Transfer credits are subject to approval by the

1.3 Supervisory Committee (SC)
1.3.1 Role of the Committee
The supervisory committee plays a key role in a graduate stu-
dent’s progress through the PhD program. In particular, the SC
(i) approves the student’s Program of Study,
(ii) supervises the student’s Candidacy Exam,2 2
The Physics Department’s Candidacy
Exam is an example of what the SGS

sive Exam.
(iv) reads the student’s dissertation, and
(v) conducts the final Dissertation Defense Examination.
Sections 1.5 and 2.3.3 discuss aspects of these steps in detail.
1.3.2 Composition of the Committee
The major professor is the chairperson of the committee and usu-
ally directs the student’s research.3 Requirements for the composition 3

• The committee must consist of three members from within the

• Adjunct faculty can be committee members with the approval of

• Emeritus faculty may continue to serve as committee members or

1.4 Dissertation Proposal
The purpose of the document known as the Dissertation Pro-
posal is to set the course for the student’s research that will appear in
the dissertation. There is some flexibility as to exactly when the pro-
posal is approved by the SC. Some major professors prefer approval
to take place as early as is possible, which typically means shortly
after the student has been engaged in enough research that the stu-
dent is able to reasonably propose a direction and scope for what will
appear in the dissertation. Other major professors prefer that the pro-
posal come later, after the dissertation research is well under way. In
either case, shortly after the successful completion of the Candidacy
exam, the student should be in conversation with the major professor
regarding expectations regarding the Dissertation Proposal.
There are no formal requirements regarding the level of detail (and
hence the length) of the proposal. Major professor’s expectations
range from a few pages to a rather lengthy document that might con-
tain a timeline, for example. Again, the student should communicate
with their major professor regarding this aspect of the document.
There is a hard deadline associated with this proposal. The Disser-
tation proposal must be approved by the SC before the ACDD form
(see Sec. 1.5 ) is submitted to the SGS, and the ACDD form must be
submitted at least 3 months before the Dissertation Defense Examina-
tion.
The Dissertation Proposal must be defended by the student
before the student’s SC. This defense must be formally scheduled
through the SGS, as detailed in Sec. 1.5.
1.5 SGS Forms – Before the Dissertation Defense
During a student’s tenure a number of SGS forms must be
filled out and signed in order to document the student’s passage
through the program. The student must work closely with the GPC
to fill out these forms The student is responsible for completing and
usu phd program – general requirements 13
submitting most of these forms. The forms can be found on the SGS
website:
School of Graduate Studies: Academic Forms.
Seven SGS forms are required prior to the student’s defense of
their dissertation.
(A) Supervisory Committee Approval Form (SCAF). This form
must be submitted to the School of Graduate Studies for ap-
proval by the end of the student’s third semester in the pro-
gram. Committee changes cannot be made during the six weeks
prior to the final defense.
(B) Program of Study (POS). In conjunction with the SC, a student
develops a program of study, which details all of the course
work and dissertation research credits that the student shall take.
This information is transmitted to the Graduate School via the
POS form. The POS form should be submitted after the SCAF
has been approved, but no later than the end of the student’s
third semester. The POS form is submitted by the departments’s
Graduate Program Coordinator (GPC).
(C) Full Time at Three Credits (FT3). After completion of all course-
work outlined in an approved POS, a student need only to reg-
ister for three credits to be considered a full-time. Use the FT3
form if you meet this criterion, and there is a reason you need to
be listed as a full-time student (for example, to defer repayment
of student loans).
(D) Appointment for Proposal Defense (AFP). This form must
be filled out in order for the student to formally defend their
dissertation proposal. It can only be filled out once the SCAF
and POS are filled out and accepted by the SGS. This form must
be filled out 10 workdays before the proposal defense date.
(E) Record of Proposal Defense (ROP). This form is filled out after
the proposal defense. It is submitted by the GPC.
(F) Application for Candidacy for a Doctoral Degree (ACDD).
After
(i) completion of Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR)
training,
(ii) passing the Physic Department’s Candidacy Examination,
and
(iii) approval of the Dissertation Proposal by the SC,

(G) Appointment for Final Defense (AFD). This form must be filled

1.6 The Dissertation
No research is complete until it is published. In many cases
the PhD work of the student will be published as articles in journals
and/or presented at conferences and meetings appropriate to the
field of study. In addition, the student is required to write a disserta-
tion on their research.

1.6.2 Defense of the Dissertation
The PhD candidate must defend their dissertation before
the SC. This is an oral defense. The following summarizes details
regarding the defense.
Requirements
• The student must be registered for 3 or more credits in the semester
they defend their dissertation, but there are exceptions, as follows.
A domestic student may be registered for 1 credit during their de-
fense semester; however, they will be dropped to part time status.
A student must maintain full time status for financial aid. Inter-
national students must be registered for 3 credits if they defend
in Fall or Spring semesters but may register for 1 credit if they are
defending in the summer session.
16 phd handbook
• All defenses are public.
• All committee members must attend the defense at the date and
time registered with the School of Graduate Studies. While in-
person defense is preferred and recommended, members of the
committee may participate remotely with both audio and video
interaction.
Before the Defense
• Students should review their official committee to make sure it is
correct. No changes in the supervisory committee are allowed
during the six weeks prior to defense.
• Students should determine when they need to have their degree
in hand. The student should work with their Major Professor, SC,
and GPC to determine a timeline for their dissertation completion.
Graduate student deadlines for final defense, graduation, and
degree posting can be reviewed on the
Graduate Studies Deadlines Page.
In order to meet the deadlines, students should submit their doc-
uments no later than 3 weeks before the dates listed on the dead-
lines page.
• During the semester the student intends to graduate, the Gradua-
tion Check Request form should be filled out and submitted.
• Students should submit their dissertation to each committee mem-
ber at least 4 weeks prior to their defense date for review.
• No committee member should agree to proceed with a defense
until they have carefully read and approved the dissertation.
• The final defense should be scheduled by the student after all
coursework in the POS is completed and the student has finished
writing the dissertation.
• Students should work with their committee members to arrange
defense participation and details prior to submitting the required
Appointment for Examination (AFE) form, which must be sub-
mitted at least 10 business days prior to their defense. The stu-
dent should check on the progress of approvals for their AFE (and
follow up with GPC and/or committee members to make sure it
is approved in a timely manner). If the AFE is not fully approved
before the date of defense, the defense is not official and will need
usu phd program – general requirements 17
to be rescheduled. Once the AFE has been approved by the SC
and the School of Graduate Studies, any changes to the date, time,
and/or location require the submission and approval of a new
AFE form.
During the Defense
• The oral examination of the dissertation is a defense of a final
document. Only minor changes—usually editorial—should be
required following the defense. If major changes are required,
a defense of the revised document should be held. The student
must be registered during the semester of a new defense.
• During the examination, the student defends their dissertation and
answers questions about the research or related topics.
• At the end of the oral dissertation defense, the SC votes to pass
or fail (or perhaps, abstain). In most cases, all members of a SC
approve a successful dissertation defense. However, a defense
is deemed successful with a vote of 4 members in favor and 1
against or abstaining. All members of the SC are required, as a
condition of committee membership, to sign the forms associated
with a successful defense, regardless of the member’s individual
vote. Committee members’ signatures reflect concurrence that all
policies and procedures of the dissertation process were followed,
including a favorable vote of 5-0 or 4-1.
• Any instances of a dissertation receiving 3 votes in favor that can-
not be resolved (to either a pass or failure) by discussion of the
committee shall be referred to the Vice Provost of Graduate Stud-
ies for resolution.
After the Defense
• The student should be informed of the defense results at the con-
clusion of the defense.
• The major professor or designated committee member should in-
form the GPC of the results of the defense as soon as possible. The
GPC will then submit the Record of Examination form in Service
Now, with the committee subsequently verifying the results of the
defense.
• The student should discuss the ownership of data and authorship
rights with the SC. Subsequently, the Format & Style Form (F&S),
18 phd handbook
Authorship & Copyright form, Title Page form, and Embargo
Request form (if so desired) should be submitted to the SGS.
These forms can be found at
School of Graduate Studies: Academic Forms.
• After submission of the above forms, the dissertation (in .pdf
format) is submitted to the Physics Department’s Reviewer, who
checks the formatting of the dissertation. Any required edits are
noted and the document is returned to the student for correc-
tions. Once the dissertation has passed the departmental review
process, the GPC uploads the document for review by the SGS.
Upon successful review by the SGS, the document is signed by the
Vice Provost for Graduate Studies and then sent to the university’s
library.
• Once the student’s dissertation has been finalized by the SGS and
has met the library requirements, the School of Graduate Studies
will verify that all degree requirements have been met.
1.7 Time Limit
A doctorate degree must be completed within eight years
of entering the degree program. Additional time may be requested
by the student’s committee and submitted to the Vice Provost of
Graduate Studies for review. Coursework more than eight years old
at the time of degree completion may not be used for a graduate
degree unless it is revalidated, as described in Sec. 1.2.

Physics PhD Program – Requirements and Guidelines
2.1 Introduction
The purpose of this section is to help students and faculty un-
derstand the specific requirements associated with the PhD program
in the Physics Department, elaborating upon the general require-
ments of the SGS discussed above (see Sec. 1). Section 2.2 succinctly
summarizes the steps involved in obtaining the PhD degree. Sections
2.3 – 2.8 describe each aspect of the PhD program in detail.
The specifics of the Physics PhD program are also summarized in
the USU General Catalog at
USU Catalog: Physics PhD.
2.2 Overview of the Physics PhD Program
The PhD program consists of the following elements, in
roughly chronological order.1 1
An explicit timeline can be found in
Sec. 3.
• Matriculation and an initial advisement meeting with the Gradu-
ate Program Coordinator (GPC), and the Graduate Student Track-
ing Committee (GSTC) to discuss PhD course requirements and
outline a preliminary program of study.
• Throughout the student’s time at USU, continued advisement/tracking
with the DA, GPC, GSTC, and the student’s Supervisory Commit-
tee (SC).
• Completion of 10 SC-approved courses. By default, 9 of these
courses are Physics Core courses. Coursework is to be completed
during the first two years of graduate study.
22 phd handbook
• Completion of the Physics Department’s Colloquium attendance
requirement (four semesters of attendance) during the first two
years in the program.
• Qualification, which consists primarily of an evaluation of the
student’s performance in physics graduate courses taken during
the first year.
• Establishment of the student’s SC, which includes the major pro-
fessor.
• A Program of Study to be developed and filed with the School of
Graduate Studies.
• A research-format Candidacy Examination.
• Research with the student’s major professor, including the disser-
tation proposal (and its defense), actual research, writing of the
dissertation, presentation of two public research seminars, and
defense of the dissertation.
• Completion of post-defense paperwork
• The time limit for completion of a PhD degree is eight years after
matriculation.
2.3 Advising and Tracking
2.3.1 Matriculation and Initial Advisement
Shortly after matriculation into the program, each PhD
student has an initial advisement meeting with the DA and GPC.
A preliminary Program of Study is explored at that time so that
coursework for the first year can be set. This initial meeting takes
place in the week before the start of classes.
physics phd program – requirements and guidelines 23
2.3.2 Continued Advisement and Tracking
The purpose of continued advisement and tracking is to
make sure that the student is satisfactorily progressing toward a
Physics PhD degree. Advisement and tracking of the graduate stu-
dents takes place continually while the student is in the program.
• Before the student has established their SC, the majority of advis-
ing is done by the GPC.
• In order to help ensure that the student is making satisfactory
progress, the GSTC will meet with each student on at least a
yearly basis, typically early in the spring semester. These meet-
ings are mandatory for each student. If the student is located
away from the university during the spring semester, a video inter-
view with the GSTC may be conducted.
• After establishment of the SC, the primary advising role is natu-
rally assumed by the student’s major professor.
2.3.3 The Supervisory Committee (SC)
The student’s SC consists of a major professor (who usually
is the main advisor to the student during the research phase of PhD
degree) and at least four other faculty members. Details of the com-
position of this committee can be found Sec. 1.3.2. The student’s SC
is the key connection between the student and the student’s success-
ful completion of the PhD degree.
The basic timeline regarding the student’s SC is outlined as fol-
lows.
• The student chooses a major professor and forms their SC during
the third semester (if not earlier).
• Shortly after formation of the SC, the student should meet with
the SC to discuss the Program of Study, including, perhaps, the
transfer of credits or waiver of certain course requirements as
discussed in Sec. 2.4.4. No later than the end of third semester the
SC approves the student’s Program of Study.
• During the fourth semester, the SC selects the specific material to
be the focus of the Candidacy Examination.
• During the fifth semester the SC participates in the Candidacy
Exam as a required primary cohort of the faculty.
24 phd handbook
• After successfully passing the Candidacy Exam, the student pre-
pares a Dissertation Proposal, which must be approved by the
SC.
• The SC, especially the major professor, mentors the student in
their dissertation research.
• The SC reads the dissertation and participates in the student’s
Dissertation Defense Examination.
Many of the above steps require the student to complete and sub-
mit an associated form to the School of Graduate Studies. These
forms can be found at
School of Graduate Studies: Academic Forms
and are detailed in Secs. 1.5 and 4.

2.4.3 Grade Requirement for PhD Courses
A minimum B average (GPA 3.0) is required for all coursework
that appears on a student’s POS. A grade of C− or less will not be
accepted for a graduate degree.
26 phd handbook
2.4.4 Possible Waiver of Course Requirements
Students who have previously taken graduate courses
at another institution that are equivalent to courses required in
Sec. 2.4.1 may
(1) ask to have their SC petition the graduate school to transfer up to
12 credits as part of their Program of Study (see Sec. 1.2) and/or
(2) ask that the previously taken courses fulfill appropriate course
requirements in Sec. 2.4.1.
Any credits transferred to the Program of Study cannot have been
used towards a previous degree. Such a student should assemble a
SC as early as possible so that the Program of Study can be approved.
The student should not assume that any previously taken graduate
courses will automatically be substituted for USU courses. It is en-
tirely up to the student’s SC to make this determination. Any such
waivers to taking USU graduate courses should be preliminarily dis-
cussed with the DA and GSTC upon entering the graduate program.
2.4.5 Program of Study Form
A Program of Study (POS) form must be filled out and filed with
the Graduate School. The student’s Program of Study is typically
developed with help from the DA, GSTC, and SC. It should be
filed with the Graduate School by the end of the student’s third
semester. This form must be approved by the SC.
2.4.6 Colloquium Requirement
Each semester the Physics Department hosts a series of
colloquia (on Tuesdays at 3:00 PM). In order to increase each stu-
dent’s appreciation of the overall endeavor of contemporary physics
research, each PhD student is required to attend each Physics De-
partment Colloquium during the first four semesters that they are
enrolled in the graduate program. In order to track attendance, each
student is required to fill out the Colloquium Response form at each
colloquium (and then leave it on the table at the back of the Confer-
ence Room at the end of the colloquium).
physics phd program – requirements and guidelines 27
2.5 Qualification
Each student enrolled in the PhD program is evaluated for
qualification for PhD work. In order that the totality of the student’s
first year in the program can be evaluated, consideration of quali-
fication occurs at the beginning of the fall semester of the second
year. Qualification of the student is primarily based on coursework,
although the qualification process may also include an evaluation of
the student’s work as a teaching assistant or research assistant.
A standardized Application for Qualification (AQ) form must
be submitted to the faculty by the student (with help from the DA)
before the faculty meet to discuss the student’s qualification.
If satisfactory progress is being made by the student, the student
shall continue in the PhD program. If not, the faculty may
(i) decide to reconsider qualification the following semester or
(ii) remove the student from the PhD program, in which case the
student may apply to the master’s program (although accep-
tance is not guaranteed).
2.6 Candidacy Examination
The Candidacy Exam consists of
(1) a written report and
(2) an oral presentation, followed by
(3) deliberation and voting by the faculty.
The examination topic should be set during the fourth semester
of the student’s program, and the examination should take place
during the student’s fifth semester.
Detailed requirements and guidelines for the examination can be
found in the document
A Guide to the Physics Candidacy Exam.
The Intent for Candidacy (ICE) Form is the required form associ-
ated with the exam. It serves two purposes.

• Page 1 of the ICE form is used to set the topic of the exam. This
part of the form should be filled out as soon as the topic is set, and
must be signed by all members of the SC.
• Page 2 is used to schedule the exam. This side must be signed by
the DA and distributed (with the written report) to the Physics
faculty (and outside member of the SC) at least 7 days before the
oral presentation. It is the responsibility of the student to ensure
that the form and written report are distributed on time.
The ICE form can be found at on the Physics Department’s website at

2.7 Student’s with a Previous Master’s Degree
Student’s with a Master’s Degree that are accepted into the
PhD program may be able to shorten their timeline for the PhD.
Whether or not this is the case largely depends upon how relevant
previous coursework is to the student’s PhD program. For example,
if a student is able to complete their coursework at USU within a year
of matriculation, then it may make sense for the student to move up
the Candidacy Exam to their 3rd semester (from the standard 5th
semester). Such potential compression of the PhD program should be
discussed with the SC as early as it possible.
2.8 Research Program
The major component of the PhD degree is the undertaking
of original research. Usually this occurs as part of the major profes-
sor’s overall research program, but often has significant input from
the student with regards to the scope and direction of the research.
There are five formal components associated with this aspect of the
student’s program, as discussed in the following subsections.
2.8.1 Responsible Conduct of Research Training
Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) is the practice of sci-
entific investigation with integrity. It involves the awareness and
application of established professional norms and ethical principles
in the performance of all activities related to scientific research. All
physics phd program – requirements and guidelines 29
PhD students are required to complete RCR training. Details about
this training can be found at
Responsible Conduct of Research Training.
2.8.2 Dissertation Proposal
The first stage of the research process is to become ac-
quainted enough with a specific area of research that a Dissertation
Proposal can be drafted and submitted to the student’s SC. Part of
this acquaintance may come via preparation for the Candidacy Ex-
amination. The Dissertation Proposal must be approved by the SC. A
more detailed discussion regarding the Dissertation Proposal can be
found in Sec. 1.4.
2.8.3 Research with the Major Professor
After approval of the Dissertation Proposal, the student
should focus on their research project. Completion of the research
project typically takes between two and four years. Utah State Uni-
versity has a policy of 8 years maximum for completion of the PhD
degree from the date of matriculation.
2.8.4 Seminar Requirement
The Physics Department requires each PhD student to present
at least two research seminars associated with their research (neither
of which can be the Candidacy Examination oral presentation). One
of these is associated with the dissertation defense (see below). The
other seminar can be a local seminar given to members of a local
research group, a presentation at a regional, national, or international
conference, or an invited talk at another institution.
2.8.5 Dissertation and Defense
After completion of the research, the student is required
to write a dissertation on the research. As part of the Dissertation
Defense, a public seminar on the material in the dissertation will be
presented. Immediately following the public seminar, the dissertation
is defended before the student’s Supervisory Committee. Paperwork
(in the form of ever more forms) is associated with the dissertation
and its defense; see Sec. 4 for details.
